To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
DDEP, TTMS, and AIA cause mechanism-based inactivations of human P450s in a manner that is consistent with their porphyrinic effects in animals.

the porphyrins DDEP, TTMS, and AIA cause mechanism-based inactivity of human P450s1A1,1A2,2C9,3A4 but not P4502D, whereas AIA is not inactivated by any of the human P45O isozymes tested.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a human P450 isoenzyme system that is capable of identifying and predicting the mechanism-based inactivation potential of xenobiotics in humans.
the development of a human model for mechanism-based inactivation and its use for extrapolation of animal studies.
elucidating the mechanisms of porphyria caused by xenobiotics in animal models and extrapolating this information to the human species.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

mechanism-based inactivation is a general mechanism by which certain xenobiotics exert their porphryinogenic effects in animal models and that this inactivation mechanism is conserved in humans, but not all xenobiotics that cause mechanism-based inactivity of animal P450 isozymess will do so in humans.
the results from cDNA-expressed isozymes are consistent with results obtained in animal models and that the results from the animal models can be extrapolated to humans with confidence.
the porphyrinic compounds DDEP and TMS inactivated human P450s in a manner that was similar to that in rat, but not chick embryo liver, whereas the porphyrinoic compound AIA did not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DDEP is a good model compound for mechanism-based inactivation in both humans and rodents, whereas AIA is a good model for inactivation in rodents but not in humans.
the results of inactivation studies on animal models should be interpreted with care when extrapolating to humans.
the P450 isozymic basis of porphyrinogen production in animals is likely to be different from the basis in humans.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mechanism-based inactivation studies in animal models are important, but the results should be supplemented with studies on cDNA expressed human P450s.
it is important to supplement studies of xenobiotics in animal models with studies on cDNA expressed human P450 isoenzymes to ensure the extrapolation of data from animal models to humans.
the inactivation of human P450 enzymes can be used as a surrogate marker for porphyrinogen production in humans.
